title: Manuscript
text:
Across three pilot studies and one main study, we examined how people annotated two forms of text: song lyrics and political speeches. We conducted pilot studies with the primary aim of estimating the number of ratings needed per text type (lyrics vs. speeches). On the basis of these pilots, we then designed four surveys: two for the annotation of lyrics and two for the annotation of speeches. As all studies shared the same overall procedure, we first describe the stimuli, survey design, and participant recruitment procedure, followed by the specific methods and results of the pilot and main studies.
Our procedures were reviewed, determined to have minimal risk to participants, and thus approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at Delft University of Technology1. The study plans and analysis were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/fhq75).
All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2025) within the RStudio integrated development environment (RStudio Team, 2025), along with the here (Müller, 2020) helper functions for managing file paths. Data wrangling and statistical analysis relied on the tidyverse suite (Wickham et al., 2019), helper functions from rlang (Henry & Wickham, 2024) and ggplot2 for visualization (Wickham, 2016). Reliability analyses were conducted with the psych package (Revelle, 2023), mixed-effects models were estimated with lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), and p values from statistical tests were estimated with lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). Additional APA formatting and reporting used gt (Iannone et al., 2023) and papaja (Aust & Barth, 2022).


See Appendix A: Stimuli for further details regarding stimuli data and sampling procedures.


We used the same initial pool of song lyric excerpts as Demetriou et al. (2024), who obtained lyrics with permission via the API of Musixmatch2. Musixmatch crowdsources lyrics by hosting a platform where users add, correct, sync, and translate the lyrics to songs, and engages in quality assurance which includes spam detection, formatting, checking spelling and translation, and manual verification, via their employee editors and a community of curators that function similarly to moderators on forums like Reddit.
Demetriou et al. (2024) aimed at gathering a diverse sample of songs by using a procedure they called “fuzzy stratified sampling”. An ideal scenario would have been to gather a representative sample of lyrics, with a pre-determined target number of songs, randomly sampled from within clearly defined strata (Groves et al., 2009). However, Demetriou et al. (2024) note that the population of songs is enormous, with many streaming services reporting over 100 million songs in their catalogues3, and that no work has been conducted to determine a target number of songs to reach saturation for the purposes of the annotation of values, or what a complete list of relevant strata should be. Further, while some strata that may relate to language use in song lyrics are conceptually clear, such as the year of release which may indicate time-appropriate slang or current events, other strata are far less clear: e.g. the year of release is a conceptually clear stratum compared to popularity for which no single ideal method for its estimation exists, which in turn is more clear than genre for which there may be some overlap in human labels, but no universally agreed upon musicological taxonomy (Liem et al., 2012), which in turn is practically more clear than the topic of the lyrics, for which topic estimation is likely to be imprecise. They thus aim for a diverse rather than a fully representative sample, by taking a stratified sampling approach while acknowledging that the strata are “fuzzy”.
Briefly, Demetriou et al. (2024) uniformally randomly sampled an initial pool of 60,000 artists in the Spotify Million Playlist Dataset (MPD)4 (Chen et al., 2018).The MPD contains the metadata of approximately 2 million individual tracks from approximately 300,000 artists, as they were arranged in playlists by users. Demetriou et al. (2024) then drew the metadata of every song from the entire discography of those 60,000 artists from the Spotify API and checked the availability of those songs in the Musixmatch database, resulting in large pool of approximately 510,000 songs from approximately 15,400 artists, and Musixmatch provided the first 30% of the lyrics of each song via their API.
From the pool of available 510,000 songs, Demetriou et al. (2024) then drew a sample of 2,200 song lyrics, the number of which was determined by their budgetary limitations. Songs were sampled within four “fuzzy” music strata: (1) year, the release date according to Musixmatch meta-data, which might contain some errors; (2) popularity, operationalized as the frequency that an artist appeared on a playlist in the MPD(Chen et al., 2018); (3) genre, estimated from topic modeling user-generated tags of artists in the MPD(Schindler et al., 2012), which were drawn from Last.fm and merged into the MPD5; and (4) lyric topic, via topic modelling on a bag-of-words representation of the lyrics data. Year of release was divided into equally spaced ordinal bins with year being divided into decades (60s, 70s, 80s etc.), popularity was divided into 7 ordinal bins which were approximately equal in terms of the number of songs in each bin, and genre and lyric topics were treated as non-ordinal categorical bins.
Demetriou et al. (2024) then manually screened songs for inclusion in the study. Screening primarily confirmed that the song metadata matched the song title and artist name if searched on the internet, and that the lyrics in the sample matched the lyrics of the song when listening to a streamed version. Screening secondarily removed songs that were (1) were more than approximately 20% non-English; (2) completely onomatopoetic or nonsense; (3) comprised of repeated single words or single phrases; or (4) consisted of too few words. Demetriou et al. (2024) selected a total of 380 songs. Authors of this work further screened songs using the same requirements until a total of 1,200 songs were considered usable. The first 800 excerpts were used in the main study, and the next 14 were used for a pilot study. As some songs lyrics contained non-lyric words, indicating e.g. section (i.e. verse or chorus), artist, or time stamp, included songs were manually corrected to only contain the song lyrics. Songs most frequently removed were non-English or contained a large number of non-English words, e.g. reggae songs written in Jamaican Patois or k-pop / j-pop which contained words in English as well as Korean or Japanese, followed by songs that had very few or single repeated words such as dance and electronic music.



We chose the U.S. State of the Union addresses as the overall corpus, as they are a long-running, formally recorded corpus of public speech, that has regularly been delivered to congress each year, by presidents of both parties. Speeches were sampled from the UVA Miller center repository6, which maintains a large archive of presidential communications including recordings as well as complete transcripts of speeches of U.S. presidents. Presidents generally gave a single State of the Union address each year of their presidency. Our samples were therefore stratified within (1) president, and (2) speech. We excluded all speeches before 1900 so as to sample language that is approximately current, and the single speech by Zachary Taylor so as not to oversample a single speech. Speeches were grouped by president so that each president contributed roughly the same number of excerpts (M=55.3). Within each president, every speech was divided into a proportional number of chunks, with presidents who gave fewer speeches contributing more chunks per speech and those with many speeches contributing fewer: 7 per speech from 2 term presidents, and 14 per speech from single term presidents. From each chunk, we then sampled the first ~200 words (ending at a sentence boundary), producing a balanced set of excerpts across presidents and their speeches. The first 300 excerpts were used in the main study, and 13 each were used in two pilot studies, 44.8% of which were from Democratic presidents (M=16 excerpts) vs. 55.2% Republican presidents (M=15 excerpts).




We aimed to gather responses that approximate the average perspective of a population, and sub-groups of that population. We chose the United States as the target population, given the prevalence of lyrics in the most popular songs7, and thus exclusively drew participants who reported residing in the United States, and that were fluent in English. To see if perspectives between sub-groups of the population varied, we recruited a sample of respondents stratified by the most common ethnicities in the US according to the 2024 US Census8, and additionally by political leaning for speeches.
Across all studies, participants were recruited using Prolific9, an online survey participant recruitment platform, to draw a sample that was stratified based on information participants report at registration, according to categories determined by Prolific. For ethnicity, these were: White, Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino, and three Asian sub-categories, East Asian, South Asian, South East Asian, which we combined into a single ‘Asian’ category. For speeches, we also recruited participants stratified by political spectrum (Conservative, Moderate, Liberal).



For complete survey materials, see see Appendix B: Survey.


The primary instrument in all surveys is the 10-item Short Schwartz Value Survey (SSVS) questionnaire developed by (Lindeman & Verkasalo, 2005), which participants completed on the Qualtrics10 survey platform. Each of the 10 questionnaire items in the SSVS is the name of a specific value in the Schwartz value inventory, along with a few descriptive words e.g. “POWER (social power, authority, wealth, influence on people and events)”. We asked participants to read the instructions from the Schwartz Value Survey11 in order to introduce the concept of personal values, and to instruct them on how to complete the questionnaire (Schwartz, 2005). The response format is a 9-point Likert scale which ranges from -1 (Opposed to their values) and 0 (Not at all Important), to 6 (Very Important) and 7 (Of Supreme Importance)(Lindeman & Verkasalo, 2005), which corresponds to the original, unbalanced likert scale in the Schwartz Value Survey (Schwartz, 2005).
Participants first completed the questionnaire about themselves to familiarize themselves with the task. Participants also completed an adapted version of the SSVS for each of the lyric or speech excerpts they rated. We used an SSVS version similar to (Demetriou et al., 2024), in which the instructions are slightly adapted for annotation. Briefly, for lyrics we asked participants to respond to the questions while considering the Speaker i.e. the person or thing whose perspective the lyrics reflect, which we distinguish from the Author of the text i.e. the person or people responsible for selection of words and their structure. In the case of speeches, we defined Speaker as the president delivering the speech, as opposed to the Author who may be the president, but may also be a team of speech writers and/or other staff, or other individuals who occasionally appear in the speech transcript.
For the annotation we make an adjustment to the likert scale of the SSVS: we present participants with a ‘Not Applicable’ response option, as we expect that excerpts of text give an incomplete picture of the values of the Speaker. Thus, we give participants the option to indicate NA to indicate “Not Applicable” if they felt no information on the value is present in the text. We thus gather 10 likert-scale responses per item (lyric / speech excerpt) being rated, one for each of the 10 Schwartz values, within a range of -1 to 7, and with possible NAs.



The set of survey components, in order, is shown in Figure 1. In order to ensure that participants understood the task, the survey (1) asked participants to complete the SSVS about themselves, (2) gave a 3-item comprehension quiz that gave feedback on the correctness of the response after each item, (3) repeated the instructions multiple times, and (4) contained an Attention Check to filter out low effort responses. For details regarding the specific wording of instructions for each component, see Appendix B: Survey.
Figure 1
Survey components




The comprehension quiz asked three questions shown in random order, each of which included a brief scenario: (1) “If you feel a SPEAKER seeks POWER above all else as a life-guiding principle, how would you respond?”, to which the correct response was at the high end of the scale (i.e. 5, 6, or 7), (2) “If you feel a SPEAKER doesn’t give any indication of how important POWER is to them in the lyrics, how would you respond?” to which a correct response was “NA”, and (3) “If you feel a SPEAKER avoids POWER more than anything else, or sees it as completely unimportant to them, how would you respond?” to which a correct response was on the lower end of the scale (i.e. -1, 0, or 1). Questions were accompanied by the single item, POWER. After each question, the survey displayed the correct response, along with a brief explanation e.g. “If you feel a SPEAKER seeks POWER above all else as a life-guiding principle, respond with a ‘7’, indicating it is of Supreme Importance to them”. Participants most often mistook “NA” and low-end scale responses in Quiz items 2 and 3. Thus, for Quiz 2 where the correct response was “NA”, 13% of participants indicated “0” and “9”% indicated “-1”, where 56% correctly indicated “NA”. Similarly in Quiz 3, 13% of participants incorrectly indicated “NA” where 50% and 20% of participants correctly indicated “-1”’ and “0” respectively. Thus, in the minds of many annotators, “NA” and the lower-end of the scale bear similar meaning.



Our survey also checked if participants were paying attention. As per Prolific guidelines, we include an attention check at the halfway point of the annotation component of the survey. The check appeared to be another song lyric, with the lyrics being instructions to participants to indicate “7” for the value of Stimulation, “0” for all other values. Participants who responded with “-1” or “NA” instead were also considered passing if they were consistent in the ratings of all values other than Stimulation. Participants who failed the attention check were returned to Prolific, and automatically replaced.



We collected a number of exploratory measures which we felt might affect participant ratings, but for which we had no specific prediction. For lyrics we asked participants “Do you think the SPEAKER and the AUTHOR are the same person?”, and “Do you recognize the song that the lyrics come from?”, and for speeches we asked participants “Do you recognize the president that delivered the speech?”, and “Which party do you think the president belongs to?”. Following the SSVS for each lyric or speech excerpt, we also assessed participant confidence in their ratings by asking “How confident are you in your ratings of these lyrics? / this speech?”, to which participants could respond on a scale from 1 (Completely Confident) to 5 (Completely Unconfident).

Results
All analysis and visualization is conducted using R [citation], and rendered via Quarto [citation]. A repository for this study can be found here [github link].

Pilot Study

Determining annotator sample strata
We estimate ICC2k overall, and for subgroups separately. For our lyrics pilot, we observe overall ‘good’ ICC2k estimates, with the exception of SELF-DIRECTION, which shows a large confidence interval that exceeds our threshold. These ICC2k scores overall do not appear to improve when we estimate them separately for each Ethnicity.

This is not the case for our two pilots which used political speech data. Overall, agreement on the speech data was unusably poor, however it appeared to improve when estimated separately for each ethnicity, with most values showing ICC2k scores over the threshold. Note that estimation for HEDONISM is generally poor in subsamples, and that STIMULATION is poor in some subsamples.

We observe similar results for our second speeches pilot, which show substantially higher ICC2k scores when they are estimated separately for each political spectrum category.


Conclusion
We tentatively conclude that Ethnicity will have a substantially smaller effect on ratings of song lyrics than either Ethnicity or Political Spectrum will have on ratings of speeches. Thus, the sample for our main study data collection will be stratified by Ethnicity, and for political speeches, it will also be stratified by political affiliation.



Estimating the number of raters
The results from our bootstrapping procedure show adequate ICC2k scores with 15 ratings for lyrics, in both ICC2k scores, and correlations between subsample means and the overall mean.

For both samples in our speech pilots, we observe a bimodal distribution in ICC2k scores, with peaks nearing our threshold, but also around 0.
Our sample of annotators in our first speeches pilot were stratified by Ethncitiy. Our bootstrapping analysis shows sufficiently high correlations between subsample means and the overall mean at around 40 ratings, however, ICC2k scores do not reach sufficiently high ICC2k scores even with 50 ratings.

Our sample of annotators in our first speeches pilot were stratified by political affiliation. We observe a similar pattern, where the correlations between subsample means and the overall mean reach our threshold 35 ratings, but ICC2k scores are not sufficiently high even with 50 ratings.


Conclusion
We thus proceed with a target median 15 ratings per song lyric excerpt. Based on bootstrapped correlations between subsamples and the overall sample, as well as budgetary constraints, we aim for median 40 ratings per political speech excerpt.

Methods

Participants and Survey Software
Our budget allowed us to compensate approximately 1700 participants for our final sample, 850 each per stimulus type (lyrics / speeches).
Quiz results: Participants most often mistook “NA” and low-end scale responses in Quiz items 2 and 3. Thus, for Quiz 2 where the correct response was “NA”, 13% of participants indicated “0” and “9”% indicated “-1”, where 56% correctly indicated “NA”. Similarly in Quiz 3, 13% of participants incorrectly indicated “NA” where 50% and 20% of participants correctly indicated “-1”’ and “0” respectively. Thus, in the minds of many annotators, “NA” and the lower-end of the scale bear similar meaning. Participants who answered 2 quiz questions incorrectly were redirected back to Prolific and partially compensated for their time. 723 participants opted to take our survey, 427 of which passed both the attention checks and the quizzes.


Main Study

Initial Validation
We take a first look at the SSVS by examining multidimensional scaling plots from participant self-ratings, and compare these to the canonical Schwartz circumplex illustration:

As an initial measure of validity, we examine multi-dimensional scaling plots (MDS) , which has previously been used as method to assess measurements conform to theory~. We compute correlations from our sample of annotations, and, from data simulated from the upper triangle of a correlation matrix reported in~. To compute the correlations from our sample, we averaged participant ratings per value, per song. To interpret the plots we observe whether there is a similar structure to that in Figure~\(\ref{fig:circle}\), and whether each value appears next to its appropriate neighbors (note: absolute position is unimportant). MDS plots (Figure~\(\ref{fig:mds_plots}\)), show promising results, although ACHIEVEMENT' appears closer toSECURITY’, and HEDONISM' andSTIMULATION’ are transposed.
We further compare to an MDS plot from the correlation matrix reported in a landmark study. In general, the aim of the test is to observe whether values appear next to the appropriate neighbor; note that absolute position is not relevant.
Although not identical, and not quite as circular as expected, we do observe most of the expected patterns. As we also see in the landmark study, not every point aligns with the canonical illustration.



Inter-rater reliability
In contrast to our pilot study, in general we observe sufficient ICC2k scores, with no visible improvement when estimated by ethnicity or political leaning.
ICC2k scores for lyrics ratings appear to be exceptionally high overall, and when estimated separately within Ethnic groups, and do not seem to improve when estimated separately for each Ethnic group.

Ratings of political speeches exceed our threshold overall, though ratings do not always meet the threshold when estimated separately within Ethnic groups. In general, the estimates are visibly worse than for lyrics. Once again, we see issues with HEDONISM being poorly estimated for one group, and STIMULATION is poorly estimated for another group.

We observe a similar pattern when separating groups by political affiliation.



MDS plots of text annotations
When examining the MDS plots for our lyrics annotations, we generally see acceptable patterns with most values appearing next to appropriate neighbors, although STIMULATION and HEDONISM appear transposed, and ACHEIVEMENT shows a shift from the perimeter of the circumplex. These patterns are visibly worse for speeches, where we observe a strong shift for HEDONISM from the perimeter of the circumplex.



Model approach selection
We then determine a general modelling approach in order to estimate the effect of Ethnicity on ratings of lyrics, and Ethnicity and Political spectrum on ratings of political speeches.
To do so we plot the observed vs. predicted values and estimate a pseudo R^2, for three models:

general linear mixed effects model (lmer)
ordinal mixed effects model (clmm)
generalized linear mixed effects logistic model (glmer)

Conclusion
Model fit was consistently worse for ordinal mixed effects models, vs. general or generalized linear mixed effects models. We thus proceed to our specification curve analysis using general mixed effects models for ease of interpretation and computation.

text:
We used the same initial pool of song lyric excerpts as Demetriou et al. (2024), who obtained lyrics with permission via the API of Musixmatch1. Musixmatch crowdsources lyrics by hosting a platform where users add, correct, sync, and translate the lyrics to songs, and engages in quality assurance which includes spam detection, formatting, checking spelling and translation, and manual verification, via their employee editors and a community of curators that function similarly to moderators on forums like Reddit.
Demetriou et al. (2024) aimed at gathering a diverse sample of songs by using a procedure they called “fuzzy stratified sampling”. An ideal scenario would have been to gather a representative sample of lyrics, with a pre-determined target number of songs, randomly sampled from within clearly defined strata (Groves et al., 2009). However, Demetriou et al. (2024) note that the population of songs is enormous, with many streaming services reporting over 100 million songs in their catalogues2, and that no work has been conducted to determine a target number of songs to reach saturation for the purposes of the annotation of values, or what a complete list of relevant strata should be. Further, while some strata that may relate to language use in song lyrics are conceptually clear, such as the year of release which may indicate time-appropriate slang or current events, other strata are far less clear: e.g. the year of release is a conceptually clear stratum compared to popularity for which no single ideal method for its estimation exists, which in turn is more clear than genre for which there may be some overlap in human labels, but no universally agreed upon musicological taxonomy (Liem et al., 2012), which in turn is practically more clear than the topic of the lyrics, for which topic estimation is likely to be imprecise. They thus aim for a diverse rather than a fully representative sample, by taking a stratified sampling approach while acknowledging that the strata are “fuzzy”.
Briefly, Demetriou et al. (2024) uniformally randomly sampled an initial pool of 60,000 artists in the Spotify Million Playlist Dataset (MPD)3 (Chen et al., 2018).The MPD contains the metadata of approximately 2 million individual tracks from approximately 300,000 artists, as they were arranged in playlists by users. Demetriou et al. (2024) then drew the metadata of every song from the entire discography of those 60,000 artists from the Spotify API and checked the availability of those songs in the Musixmatch database, resulting in large pool of approximately 510,000 songs from approximately 15,400 artists, and Musixmatch provided the first 30% of the lyrics of each song via their API.
From the pool of available 510,000 songs, Demetriou et al. (2024) then drew a sample of 2,200 song lyrics, the number of which was determined by their budgetary limitations. Songs were sampled within four “fuzzy” music strata: (1) year, the release date according to Musixmatch meta-data, which might contain some errors; (2) popularity, operationalized as the frequency that an artist appeared on a playlist in the MPD(Chen et al., 2018); (3) genre, estimated from topic modeling user-generated tags of artists in the MPD(Schindler et al., 2012), which were drawn from Last.fm and merged into the MPD4; and (4) lyric topic, via topic modelling on a bag-of-words representation of the lyrics data. Year of release was divided into equally spaced ordinal bins with year being divided into decades (60s, 70s, 80s etc.), popularity was divided into 7 ordinal bins which were approximately equal in terms of the number of songs in each bin, and genre and lyric topics were treated as non-ordinal categorical bins.
Demetriou et al. (2024) then manually screened songs for inclusion in the study. Screening primarily confirmed that the song metadata matched the song title and artist name if searched on the internet, and that the lyrics in the sample matched the lyrics of the song when listening to a streamed version. Screening secondarily removed songs that were (1) were more than approximately 20% non-English; (2) completely onomatopoetic or nonsense; (3) comprised of repeated single words or single phrases; or (4) consisted of too few words. Demetriou et al. (2024) selected a total of 380 songs. Authors of this work further screened songs using the same requirements until a total of 1,200 songs were considered usable. The first 800 excerpts were used in the main study, and the next 14 were used for a pilot study. As some songs lyrics contained non-lyric words, indicating e.g. section (i.e. verse or chorus), artist, or time stamp, included songs were manually corrected to only contain the song lyrics. Songs most frequently removed were non-English or contained a large number of non-English words, e.g. reggae songs written in Jamaican Patois or k-pop / j-pop which contained words in English as well as Korean or Japanese, followed by songs that had very few or single repeated words such as dance and electronic music. See Appendix A: Stimuli for further details regarding the lyrics stimuli data and sampling procedure.



We chose the U.S. State of the Union addresses as the overall corpus, as they are a long-running, formally recorded corpus of public speech, that has regularly been delivered to congress each year, by presidents of both parties. Speeches were sampled from the UVA Miller center repository5, which maintains a large archive of presidential communications including recordings as well as complete transcripts of speeches of U.S. presidents. Presidents generally gave a single State of the Union address each year of their presidency. Our samples were therefore stratified within (1) president, and (2) speech. We excluded all speeches before 1900 so as to sample language that is approximately current, and the single speech by Zachary Taylor so as not to oversample a single speech. Speeches were grouped by president so that each president contributed roughly the same number of excerpts (M=55.3). Within each president, every speech was divided into a proportional number of chunks, with presidents who gave fewer speeches contributing more chunks per speech and those with many speeches contributing fewer: 7 per speech from 2 term presidents, and 14 per speech from single term presidents. From each chunk, we then sampled the first ~200 words (ending at a sentence boundary), producing a balanced set of excerpts across presidents and their speeches. The first 300 excerpts were used in the main study, and 13 each were used in two pilot studies, 44.8% of which were from Democratic presidents (M=16 excerpts) vs. 55.2% Republican presidents (M=15 excerpts). See Appendix A: Stimuli for further details regarding the speech stimuli data and sampling procedure.

Sampling Lyrics Excerpts

Bias Correction Procedure
Demetriou et al. (2024) observed a skew in data concentration such that songs that were recent and artists that appeared very frequently in playlists were most likely be sampled. To compensate, Demetriou et al. (2024) oversampled less populated bins by increasing the probability that songs in underpopulated bins are selected, using a maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimate of the categorical distribution of each stratum (Bassett & Deride, 2019). Oversampling is controlled via a concentration parameter \(a\) of the symmetric Dirichlet distribution which was heuristically set to 40,000, with the aim of between 5% and 10% of the overall pool of 2200 songs being drawn from underpopulated bins.

Political Speech Stimuli
We sampled U.S. State of the Union addresses (post-1900) from the UVA Miller Center archive. Speeches were sampled across two strata: (1) President and (2) speech, both of which were labelled by the Miller center. Speeches were stratified by president and by individual address so that each president contributed a comparable number of excerpts. Presidents with fewer addresses contributed more chunks per speech, while those with many addresses contributed fewer. Each chunk yielded the first ~200 words (ending at a sentence boundary), producing an approximately balanced set of excerpts across presidents and speeches. The final pool comprised 300 excerpts for the main study and 13 each for two pilot studies. Details of the average number of excerpts by party for both the initial pool and sample are shown in Table 5. Visualization of number of speeches per president are shown in Figure 5.

text:
Survey
For complete survey materials, see see Appendix B: Survey. The following procedure was reviewed, determined to have minimal risk to participants, and thus approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at Delft University of Technology6 for all surveys described herein.

Adapted Short Schwartz Value Survey
The primary instrument in all surveys is the 10-item Short Schwartz Value Survey (SSVS) questionnaire developed by (Lindeman & Verkasalo, 2005), which participants completed on the Qualtrics7 survey platform. Each of the 10 questionnaire items in the SSVS is the name of a specific value in the Schwartz value inventory, along with a few descriptive words e.g. “POWER (social power, authority, wealth, influence on people and events)”. We asked participants to read the instructions from the Schwartz Value Survey8 in order to introduce the concept of personal values, and to instruct them on how to complete the questionnaire (Schwartz, 2005). The response format is a 9-point Likert scale which ranges from -1 (Opposed to their values) and 0 (Not at all Important), to 6 (Very Important) and 7 (Of Supreme Importance)(Lindeman & Verkasalo, 2005), which corresponds to the original, unbalanced likert scale in the Schwartz Value Survey (Schwartz, 2005).
Participants first completed the questionnaire about themselves to familiarize themselves with the task. Participants also completed an adapted version of the SSVS for each of the lyric or speech excerpts they rated. We used an SSVS version similar to (Demetriou et al., 2024), in which the instructions are slightly adapted for annotation. Briefly, for lyrics we asked participants to respond to the questions while considering the Speaker i.e. the person or thing whose perspective the lyrics reflect, which we distinguish from the Author of the text i.e. the person or people responsible for selection of words and their structure. In the case of speeches, we defined Speaker as the president delivering the speech, as opposed to the Author who may be the president, but may also be a team of speech writers and/or other staff, or other individuals who occasionally appear in the speech transcript.
For the annotation we make an adjustment to the likert scale of the SSVS: we present participants with a ‘Not Applicable’ response option, as we expect that excerpts of text give an incomplete picture of the values of the Speaker. Thus, we give participants the option to indicate NA to indicate “Not Applicable” if they felt no information on the value is present in the text. We thus gather 10 likert-scale responses per item (lyric / speech excerpt) being rated, one for each of the 10 Schwartz values, within a range of -1 to 7, and with possible NAs.


Survey Flow
The set of survey components, in order, is shown in Figure 1. In order to ensure that participants understood the task, the survey (1) asked participants to complete the SSVS about themselves, (2) gave a 3-item comprehension quiz that gave feedback on the correctness of the response after each item, (3) repeated the instructions multiple times, and (4) contained an Attention Check to filter out low effort responses. For details regarding the specific wording of instructions for each component, see Appendix B: Survey.
Figure 1
Survey components


Comprehension Quiz
The comprehension quiz asked three questions shown in random order, each of which included a brief scenario: (1) “If you feel a SPEAKER seeks POWER above all else as a life-guiding principle, how would you respond?”, to which the correct response was at the high end of the scale (i.e. 5, 6, or 7), (2) “If you feel a SPEAKER doesn’t give any indication of how important POWER is to them in the lyrics, how would you respond?” to which a correct response was “NA”, and (3) “If you feel a SPEAKER avoids POWER more than anything else, or sees it as completely unimportant to them, how would you respond?” to which a correct response was on the lower end of the scale (i.e. -1, 0, or 1). Questions were accompanied by the single item, POWER. After each question, the survey displayed the correct response, along with a brief explanation e.g. “If you feel a SPEAKER seeks POWER above all else as a life-guiding principle, respond with a ‘7’, indicating it is of Supreme Importance to them”. Participants most often mistook “NA” and low-end scale responses in Quiz items 2 and 3. Thus, for Quiz 2 where the correct response was “NA”, 13% of participants indicated “0” and “9”% indicated “-1”, where 56% correctly indicated “NA”. Similarly in Quiz 3, 13% of participants incorrectly indicated “NA” where 50% and 20% of participants correctly indicated “-1”’ and “0” respectively. Thus, in the minds of many annotators, “NA” and the lower-end of the scale bear similar meaning.


Attention Check
Our survey also checked if participants were paying attention. As per Prolific guidelines, we include an attention check at the halfway point of the annotation component of the survey. The check appeared to be another song lyric, with the lyrics being instructions to participants to indicate “7” for the value of Stimulation, “0” for all other values. Participants who responded with “-1” or “NA” instead were also considered passing if they were consistent in the ratings of all values other than Stimulation. Participants who failed the attention check were returned to Prolific, and automatically replaced.


Exploratory Measures
We collected a number of exploratory measures which we felt might affect participant ratings, but for which we had no specific prediction. For lyrics we asked participants “Do you think the SPEAKER and the AUTHOR are the same person?”, and “Do you recognize the song that the lyrics come from?”, and for speeches we asked participants “Do you recognize the president that delivered the speech?”, and “Which party do you think the president belongs to?”. Following the SSVS for each lyric or speech excerpt, we also assessed participant confidence in their ratings by asking “How confident are you in your ratings of these lyrics? / this speech?”, to which participants could respond on a scale from 1 (Completely Confident) to 5 (Completely Unconfident).

Lyrics

text:
Pilot Studies
The primary aim of our pilot studies was to estimate the number of ratings needed per stimulus. We estimated the target number of ratings separately per text type (lyrics / speeches) as we expected that each form of text could vary in terms of degree of ambiguity. To do so, we followed a procedure similar to DeBruine & Jones (2018). This process essentially involves gathering data comprised of a) a relatively large number of ratings, on b) a relatively small sub-sample of the items to be rated, followed by bootstrapping estimates of inter-rater reliability on a range of different possible numbers of ratings. Doing so shows a sampling distribution of inter-rater reliability estimates for e.g. 5 vs. 10 vs. 15 ratings per stimulus, allowing for an estimate of a target number of ratings to achieve a target inter-rater reliability. We bootstrapped estimates of inter-rater reliability by incrementally sub-sampling numbers of raters, 50 times per increment, and then estimating a) the Pearson correlation between the sub-sample increment mean and the overall sample mean, and b) inter-rater reliability (DeBruine & Jones, 2018). We sub-sampled in increments of 5, ranging from 5 to 50, with replacement, 50 times for each increment: i.e. we sampled 5 raters 50 times, 10 raters 50 times, 15 raters 50 times etc. up to 50 raters 50 times, all with replacement.
As we aim to represent the mean of a population of raters, we estimate inter-rater reliability as ‘general consensus’ (as opposed to ‘absolute agreement’) via intraclass correlation coefficient ICC(2,k)(Koo & Li, 2016). The ‘2’ indicates two-way random effects, in that both the targets of the ratings and the raters are treated as random samples from a larger population, and the ‘k’ indicates the reliabiliity of the average of k raters. In essence, ICC2k estimates how consistently a group mean rating of k raters reflects the “true” score of each item. We used a value of 0.75 as a threshold to indicate sufficent, or “good”, agreement (Koo & Li, 2016). Thus, for a given number of raters, we estimate a sampling distribution representing their degree of general consensus, and whether the the mean consensus exceeds the 0.75 threshold. Although we did not see a recommended threshold for pearson correlations in (DeBruine & Jones, 2018), we set a threshold of 0.9 to indicate sufficient, or “high” correlation between sub-sample and overall sample means.

Participants
We recruited a total of 300 participants: 100 each stratified by ethnicity completed the lyrics and the first speeches pilot, and 100 participants stratified by political orientation completed the second speeches pilot. 1 participant each in the pilot study using lyrics and the first using speeches withdrew their data at the time this manuscript was written, as did 2 participants in the second pilot using speeches (see Table 1). title: Manuscript
text:
Across three pilot studies and one main study, we examined how people annotated two forms of text: song lyrics and political speeches. We conducted pilot studies with the primary aim of estimating the number of ratings needed per text type (lyrics vs. speeches). On the basis of these pilots, we then designed four surveys: two for the annotation of lyrics and two for the annotation of speeches. As all studies shared the same overall procedure, we first describe the stimuli, survey design, and participant recruitment procedure, followed by the specific methods and results of the pilot and main studies.
Our procedures were reviewed, determined to have minimal risk to participants, and thus approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at Delft University of Technology1. The study plans and analysis were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/fhq75).
All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2025) within the RStudio integrated development environment (RStudio Team, 2025), along with the here (Müller, 2020) helper functions for managing file paths. Data wrangling and statistical analysis relied on the tidyverse suite (Wickham et al., 2019), helper functions from rlang (Henry & Wickham, 2024) and ggplot2 for visualization (Wickham, 2016). Reliability analyses were conducted with the psych package (Revelle, 2023), mixed-effects models were estimated with lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), and p values from statistical tests were estimated with lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). Additional APA formatting and reporting used gt (Iannone et al., 2023) and papaja (Aust & Barth, 2022).


See Appendix A: Stimuli for further details regarding stimuli data and sampling procedures.


We used the same initial pool of song lyric excerpts as Demetriou et al. (2024), who obtained lyrics with permission via the API of Musixmatch2. Musixmatch crowdsources lyrics by hosting a platform where users add, correct, sync, and translate the lyrics to songs, and engages in quality assurance which includes spam detection, formatting, checking spelling and translation, and manual verification, via their employee editors and a community of curators that function similarly to moderators on forums like Reddit.
Demetriou et al. (2024) aimed at gathering a diverse sample of songs by using a procedure they called “fuzzy stratified sampling”. An ideal scenario would have been to gather a representative sample of lyrics, with a pre-determined target number of songs, randomly sampled from within clearly defined strata (Groves et al., 2009). However, Demetriou et al. (2024) note that the population of songs is enormous, with many streaming services reporting over 100 million songs in their catalogues3, and that no work has been conducted to determine a target number of songs to reach saturation for the purposes of the annotation of values, or what a complete list of relevant strata should be. Further, while some strata that may relate to language use in song lyrics are conceptually clear, such as the year of release which may indicate time-appropriate slang or current events, other strata are far less clear: e.g. the year of release is a conceptually clear stratum compared to popularity for which no single ideal method for its estimation exists, which in turn is more clear than genre for which there may be some overlap in human labels, but no universally agreed upon musicological taxonomy (Liem et al., 2012), which in turn is practically more clear than the topic of the lyrics, for which topic estimation is likely to be imprecise. They thus aim for a diverse rather than a fully representative sample, by taking a stratified sampling approach while acknowledging that the strata are “fuzzy”.
Briefly, Demetriou et al. (2024) uniformally randomly sampled an initial pool of 60,000 artists in the Spotify Million Playlist Dataset (MPD)4 (Chen et al., 2018).The MPD contains the metadata of approximately 2 million individual tracks from approximately 300,000 artists, as they were arranged in playlists by users. Demetriou et al. (2024) then drew the metadata of every song from the entire discography of those 60,000 artists from the Spotify API and checked the availability of those songs in the Musixmatch database, resulting in large pool of approximately 510,000 songs from approximately 15,400 artists, and Musixmatch provided the first 30% of the lyrics of each song via their API.
From the pool of available 510,000 songs, Demetriou et al. (2024) then drew a sample of 2,200 song lyrics, the number of which was determined by their budgetary limitations. Songs were sampled within four “fuzzy” music strata: (1) year, the release date according to Musixmatch meta-data, which might contain some errors; (2) popularity, operationalized as the frequency that an artist appeared on a playlist in the MPD(Chen et al., 2018); (3) genre, estimated from topic modeling user-generated tags of artists in the MPD(Schindler et al., 2012), which were drawn from Last.fm and merged into the MPD5; and (4) lyric topic, via topic modelling on a bag-of-words representation of the lyrics data. Year of release was divided into equally spaced ordinal bins with year being divided into decades (60s, 70s, 80s etc.), popularity was divided into 7 ordinal bins which were approximately equal in terms of the number of songs in each bin, and genre and lyric topics were treated as non-ordinal categorical bins.
Demetriou et al. (2024) then manually screened songs for inclusion in the study. Screening primarily confirmed that the song metadata matched the song title and artist name if searched on the internet, and that the lyrics in the sample matched the lyrics of the song when listening to a streamed version. Screening secondarily removed songs that were (1) were more than approximately 20% non-English; (2) completely onomatopoetic or nonsense; (3) comprised of repeated single words or single phrases; or (4) consisted of too few words. Demetriou et al. (2024) selected a total of 380 songs. Authors of this work further screened songs using the same requirements until a total of 1,200 songs were considered usable. The first 800 excerpts were used in the main study, and the next 14 were used for a pilot study. As some songs lyrics contained non-lyric words, indicating e.g. section (i.e. verse or chorus), artist, or time stamp, included songs were manually corrected to only contain the song lyrics. Songs most frequently removed were non-English or contained a large number of non-English words, e.g. reggae songs written in Jamaican Patois or k-pop / j-pop which contained words in English as well as Korean or Japanese, followed by songs that had very few or single repeated words such as dance and electronic music.



We chose the U.S. State of the Union addresses as the overall corpus, as they are a long-running, formally recorded corpus of public speech, that has regularly been delivered to congress each year, by presidents of both parties. Speeches were sampled from the UVA Miller center repository6, which maintains a large archive of presidential communications including recordings as well as complete transcripts of speeches of U.S. presidents. Presidents generally gave a single State of the Union address each year of their presidency. Our samples were therefore stratified within (1) president, and (2) speech. We excluded all speeches before 1900 so as to sample language that is approximately current, and the single speech by Zachary Taylor so as not to oversample a single speech. Speeches were grouped by president so that each president contributed roughly the same number of excerpts (M=55.3). Within each president, every speech was divided into a proportional number of chunks, with presidents who gave fewer speeches contributing more chunks per speech and those with many speeches contributing fewer: 7 per speech from 2 term presidents, and 14 per speech from single term presidents. From each chunk, we then sampled the first ~200 words (ending at a sentence boundary), producing a balanced set of excerpts across presidents and their speeches. The first 300 excerpts were used in the main study, and 13 each were used in two pilot studies, 44.8% of which were from Democratic presidents (M=16 excerpts) vs. 55.2% Republican presidents (M=15 excerpts).




We aimed to gather responses that approximate the average perspective of a population, and sub-groups of that population. We chose the United States as the target population, given the prevalence of lyrics in the most popular songs7, and thus exclusively drew participants who reported residing in the United States, and that were fluent in English. To see if perspectives between sub-groups of the population varied, we recruited a sample of respondents stratified by the most common ethnicities in the US according to the 2024 US Census8, and additionally by political leaning for speeches.
Across all studies, participants were recruited using Prolific9, an online survey participant recruitment platform, to draw a sample that was stratified based on information participants report at registration, according to categories determined by Prolific. For ethnicity, these were: White, Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino, and three Asian sub-categories, East Asian, South Asian, South East Asian, which we combined into a single ‘Asian’ category. For speeches, we also recruited participants stratified by political spectrum (Conservative, Moderate, Liberal).



For complete survey materials, see see Appendix B: Survey.


The primary instrument in all surveys is the 10-item Short Schwartz Value Survey (SSVS) questionnaire developed by (Lindeman & Verkasalo, 2005), which participants completed on the Qualtrics10 survey platform. Each of the 10 questionnaire items in the SSVS is the name of a specific value in the Schwartz value inventory, along with a few descriptive words e.g. “POWER (social power, authority, wealth, influence on people and events)”. We asked participants to read the instructions from the Schwartz Value Survey11 in order to introduce the concept of personal values, and to instruct them on how to complete the questionnaire (Schwartz, 2005). The response format is a 9-point Likert scale which ranges from -1 (Opposed to their values) and 0 (Not at all Important), to 6 (Very Important) and 7 (Of Supreme Importance)(Lindeman & Verkasalo, 2005), which corresponds to the original, unbalanced likert scale in the Schwartz Value Survey (Schwartz, 2005).
Participants first completed the questionnaire about themselves to familiarize themselves with the task. Participants also completed an adapted version of the SSVS for each of the lyric or speech excerpts they rated. We used an SSVS version similar to (Demetriou et al., 2024), in which the instructions are slightly adapted for annotation. Briefly, for lyrics we asked participants to respond to the questions while considering the Speaker i.e. the person or thing whose perspective the lyrics reflect, which we distinguish from the Author of the text i.e. the person or people responsible for selection of words and their structure. In the case of speeches, we defined Speaker as the president delivering the speech, as opposed to the Author who may be the president, but may also be a team of speech writers and/or other staff, or other individuals who occasionally appear in the speech transcript.
For the annotation we make an adjustment to the likert scale of the SSVS: we present participants with a ‘Not Applicable’ response option, as we expect that excerpts of text give an incomplete picture of the values of the Speaker. Thus, we give participants the option to indicate NA to indicate “Not Applicable” if they felt no information on the value is present in the text. We thus gather 10 likert-scale responses per item (lyric / speech excerpt) being rated, one for each of the 10 Schwartz values, within a range of -1 to 7, and with possible NAs.



The set of survey components, in order, is shown in Figure 1. In order to ensure that participants understood the task, the survey (1) asked participants to complete the SSVS about themselves, (2) gave a 3-item comprehension quiz that gave feedback on the correctness of the response after each item, (3) repeated the instructions multiple times, and (4) contained an Attention Check to filter out low effort responses. For details regarding the specific wording of instructions for each component, see Appendix B: Survey.

The comprehension quiz asked three questions shown in random order, each of which included a brief scenario: (1) “If you feel a SPEAKER seeks POWER above all else as a life-guiding principle, how would you respond?”, to which the correct response was at the high end of the scale (i.e. 5, 6, or 7), (2) “If you feel a SPEAKER doesn’t give any indication of how important POWER is to them in the lyrics, how would you respond?” to which a correct response was “NA”, and (3) “If you feel a SPEAKER avoids POWER more than anything else, or sees it as completely unimportant to them, how would you respond?” to which a correct response was on the lower end of the scale (i.e. -1, 0, or 1). Questions were accompanied by the single item, POWER. After each question, the survey displayed the correct response, along with a brief explanation e.g. “If you feel a SPEAKER seeks POWER above all else as a life-guiding principle, respond with a ‘7’, indicating it is of Supreme Importance to them”. Participants most often mistook “NA” and low-end scale responses in Quiz items 2 and 3. Thus, for Quiz 2 where the correct response was “NA”, 13% of participants indicated “0” and “9”% indicated “-1”, where 56% correctly indicated “NA”. Similarly in Quiz 3, 13% of participants incorrectly indicated “NA” where 50% and 20% of participants correctly indicated “-1”’ and “0” respectively. Thus, in the minds of many annotators, “NA” and the lower-end of the scale bear similar meaning.



Our survey also checked if participants were paying attention. As per Prolific guidelines, we include an attention check at the halfway point of the annotation component of the survey. The check appeared to be another song lyric, with the lyrics being instructions to participants to indicate “7” for the value of Stimulation, “0” for all other values. Participants who responded with “-1” or “NA” instead were also considered passing if they were consistent in the ratings of all values other than Stimulation. Participants who failed the attention check were returned to Prolific, and automatically replaced.



We collected a number of exploratory measures which we felt might affect participant ratings, but for which we had no specific prediction. For lyrics we asked participants “Do you think the SPEAKER and the AUTHOR are the same person?”, and “Do you recognize the song that the lyrics come from?”, and for speeches we asked participants “Do you recognize the president that delivered the speech?”, and “Which party do you think the president belongs to?”. Following the SSVS for each lyric or speech excerpt, we also assessed participant confidence in their ratings by asking “How confident are you in your ratings of these lyrics? / this speech?”, to which participants could respond on a scale from 1 (Completely Confident) to 5 (Completely Unconfident).
